```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A heterogeneous transition network needs two pieces of information that
ordinary event logs store in different ways: the order of the coded events
within each session, and the actor type that owns each code. Some studies
keep one table per actor, because the two streams were coded separately (the
messages of a learner and the replies of a chatbot, for example); others keep
one table of all events with a column naming the actor; and others keep the
events in one table and the coding scheme, which assigns every code to an
actor, in a codebook. The analysis should not depend on which of these
layouts the data happen to arrive in.

`build_htna()` accepts all three layouts and resolves them to the same
interleaved sequence per session, so the resulting networks are identical.
This guide shows each layout on the bundled data, verifies that they give the
same network, and then covers two arguments that work with any layout:
`disambiguate`, for a code label used by more than one actor, and `group`,
for one network per cohort of sessions. Fitted clustering results are a
fourth kind of input, covered in [Clustering inputs](clustering.html).

```{r package}
library(htna)
```

## Data

The package ships the same vibe-coding sessions (429 sessions of
human-AI pair programming) in the three layouts.

- **`human_simplified`, `ai_simplified`**: one long table per actor; each
  row is one coded event of that actor.
- **`human_ai`**: both tables stacked, with the actor in `actor_type`
  (`"Human"` or `"AI"`) and a session-level cohort tag `phase` (`"Early"`,
  `"Late"`).
- **`human_ai_codebook`**: the coding scheme, one row per code, with columns
  `code` and `actor_type`.

All tables share the columns `build_htna()` reads by default:

- **Session**: `session_id` (argument `session`).
- **Code**: `code` (argument `action`).
- **Order**: `order_in_session` (argument `order`), a time index shared by
  both actors within a session, so the two streams interleave in the order
  in which the events happened.

```{r data}
data(human_ai, human_simplified, ai_simplified, human_ai_codebook)
human_ai_codebook
```

The codebook assigns six codes to each actor: the human specifies, requests,
checks, inquires, refines and expresses frustration; the AI delegates, plans,
executes, asks, repairs and reports.

## One table per actor

When each actor's events are in a separate table, the tables are passed as a
named list. The names become the actor types, in the order given.

```{r form-list}
net_list <- build_htna(list(Human = human_simplified, AI = ai_simplified))
summary(net_list)
```

The network has 12 nodes, six per actor, built from 429 sessions. Of the 144
possible directed edges 135 are non-zero, and the edge counts by actor show
that transitions occur in every block: 35 within the human codes, 36 from
human to AI, 36 from AI to human and 28 within the AI codes.

## One table with an actor column

When all events are in one table, the column that names the actor of each row
is passed as `actor_type`. The actor order follows the levels of that column
if it is a factor, and the order of first appearance otherwise.

```{r form-actor-type}
net_actor_type <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type")
```

## One table and a codebook

When the event table has no actor column, the assignment of codes to actors
is declared with `node_groups`, either as a named list of codes or as a
two-column codebook whose code column is named like `action` (here `code`).

```{r form-node-groups}
net_codes <- build_htna(
  human_ai,
  node_groups = list(
    Human = c("Specify", "Request", "Frustrate", "Check", "Inquire", "Refine"),
    AI    = c("Delegate", "Plan", "Execute", "Ask", "Repair", "Report")
  )
)
net_codebook <- build_htna(human_ai, node_groups = human_ai_codebook)
```

A code in the data that is missing from `node_groups`, or listed under two
actors, raises an error, so the declared scheme is checked against the data.

## Do the layouts give the same network?

The edge table of a network (`as.data.frame()`) lists every non-zero
transition with its weight and the actors of its two codes. If the four
networks agree, their edge tables are equal.

```{r same-network}
edges_list <- as.data.frame(net_list)
all.equal(edges_list, as.data.frame(net_actor_type))
all.equal(edges_list, as.data.frame(net_codes))
all.equal(edges_list, as.data.frame(net_codebook))
```

All three comparisons return `TRUE`: the 135 edges, their weights and their
actor assignments are the same whichever layout the data came in. The choice
of layout is therefore a matter of how the data are stored, not of the
analysis. A named list of networks is drawn one network per element:

```{r plot-forms, fig.height = 6}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
plot_htna(list(list = net_list, actor_type = net_actor_type,
               node_groups = net_codes, codebook = net_codebook))
par(op)
```

The four panels are indistinguishable, as the edge tables predicted.

## What if two actors use the same code label?

Some coding schemes give the same label to a move of either actor, for
example `Ask` for a question from the human and a clarification request from
the AI. Such codes are different behaviours, and merging them into one node
would mix the two actors. `build_htna()` therefore stops when a label occurs
under more than one actor. The small table below has `Ask` and `Reply` for
both actors in each of three sessions.

```{r overlap-data}
overlap <- data.frame(
  session_id       = rep(c("s1", "s2", "s3"), each = 6),
  code             = rep(c("Ask", "Reply", "Ask", "Reply", "Ask", "Reply"), 3),
  actor_type       = rep(c("Human", "Human", "AI", "AI", "Human", "AI"), 3),
  order_in_session = rep(seq_len(6), 3)
)
```

Building the network as usual raises an error of class
`htna_actor_conflict` that names the shared labels.

```{r overlap-error, error = TRUE}
build_htna(overlap, actor_type = "actor_type")
```

With `disambiguate = TRUE` every code is prefixed with its actor, so the two
`Ask` codes become the separate nodes `Human:Ask` and `AI:Ask`.

```{r overlap-fixed}
net_dis <- build_htna(overlap, actor_type = "actor_type",
                      disambiguate = TRUE)
as.data.frame(net_dis, what = "nodes")
```

The network has four nodes, two per actor, and each keeps its actor type.

## How is one network built per cohort?

Any layout can be split into one network per cohort of sessions with
`group`, which names a session-level column. `human_ai` has the column
`phase`, which places the first 214 sessions in chronological order in
`Early` and the remaining 215 in `Late`. The result is a grouped network
(an `htna_group`) whose cohorts follow the factor levels of `phase`.

```{r group}
grp <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type", group = "phase")
as.data.frame(summary(grp), what = "actor_pairs")
```

Both cohorts have the same actor partition; the early network has 28
non-zero AI-to-AI edges and the late network 27, and the other blocks have
the same counts in both. A grouped network is passed as it is to the other
functions (`plot_htna()`, `bootstrap_htna()`, `permutation_htna()`,
`compare_htna()` and the rest), which work through its cohorts. The
[Grouped heterogeneous transition networks](grouped.html) vignette and the
[Comparing networks](comparing-networks.html) guide continue from here.

```{r plot-group, fig.height = 4.5}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
plot_htna(grp)
par(op)
```

## Which layout to use

| Data at hand | Call |
|---|---|
| One table per actor | `build_htna(list(Human = h, AI = a))` |
| One table with an actor column | `build_htna(d, actor_type = "actor_type")` |
| One table and a codebook | `build_htna(d, node_groups = codebook)` |
| One table and code lists | `build_htna(d, node_groups = list(Human = ..., AI = ...))` |
| A fitted clustering of sessions | `build_htna(fit)`; see [Clustering inputs](clustering.html) |
| A label shared by two actors | add `disambiguate = TRUE` |
| One network per cohort | add `group = "phase"` |

```{r restore-options, include = FALSE}
options(old_options)
```
